subject: Mathematics

unit.unitTitle: Number and the Laws of Arithmetic
unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 17! In this unit you will discover the hidden rules that make arithmetic work. You already know how to add, subtract, multiply and divide. Now you will learn *why* certain shortcuts are allowed, and how a handful of powerful laws let you calculate faster, more cleverly, and with far fewer mistakes. These are the same rules that engineers, shopkeepers and computers all rely on every single day.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Mathematics 0096 — Stage 5 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: Use the commutative law to reorder additions and multiplications and make them easier.
Use the associative law to regroup numbers so that friendly pairs come together.
Use the distributive law to break a number apart for quick mental multiplication.
Follow the correct order of operations using BIDMAS.
Explain why each law works, and know when it does and does not apply.
Spot and correct common calculation errors using mathematical reasoning.
Choose the most efficient method for any calculation you meet.

concepts.title: Why We Need Laws of Arithmetic
concepts.explanation:
A mathematical law is a rule that is *always* true, no matter which numbers you use. It is not a trick that works by luck; it is a pattern built into how numbers behave. These laws do four useful jobs for you:

They let you calculate more quickly by choosing an easier path to the answer.

They help you check whether an answer is sensible.

They help you understand why shortcuts work, so you can invent your own.

They are the rules that calculators and computers are built to follow.

Let us see a law in action before we even name it. Suppose Omar needs 19 × 2 × 5 cups for a family gathering. He could work left to right: 19 × 2 = 38, then 38 × 5 = 190. That works, but the middle step is a little heavy. His sister Khadija spots something cleverer. She notices that 2 × 5 = 10, and multiplying by 10 is very easy. So she works out 19 × (2 × 5) = 19 × 10 = 190. Same answer, far less effort. Khadija did not use magic – she used the associative law, which you will meet soon.

This is the heart of the whole unit: there is often more than one correct road to the same answer, and the laws of arithmetic help you choose the smoothest road. A good mathematician is not simply someone who can grind through a calculation – it is someone who pauses, looks for a friendly pattern, and picks the easy route. Throughout this unit you will train your eyes to spot those patterns.
concepts.example: Long ago, people calculated with an abacus and with piles of stones. They noticed patterns like 1 + 9 = 10, 2 + 8 = 10, 3 + 7 = 10 and 4 + 6 = 10, and they used these pairs that make ten to add long lists quickly. Those ancient patterns are the great-grandparents of the laws you are about to learn. The maths has not changed; we have simply given the patterns clear names.

concepts.title: The Commutative Law
concepts.explanation:
The commutative law says that the order does not matter when you add or when you multiply. You can swap the numbers around and the answer stays exactly the same.

For addition: 7 + 38 = 38 + 7 = 45, and 25 + 17 = 17 + 25 = 42. For multiplication: 6 × 9 = 9 × 6 = 54, and 25 × 4 = 4 × 25 = 100. In symbols we write a + b = b + a and a × b = b × a, where the letters can stand for any numbers.

Why is this useful? Because one order is often much easier to think about than the other. Take 7 + 38. Starting at 7 and counting on 38 is slow. But by the commutative law we may write it as 38 + 7, and counting on 7 from 38 is quick and safe: 38 + 7 = 45. We chose the easier order without changing the answer.

Here is another. To work out 25 × 8, some learners find it hard to picture 25 lots of 8. But 25 × 8 = 8 × 25, and 8 lots of 25 is friendlier because 25s are like quarters of 100: four 25s make 100, so eight 25s make 200. The commutative law let us swap to the easier picture.

A gentle memory aid: the word commutative sounds like commute, which means to travel back and forth, the way Idris commutes between his home and the masjid. Numbers are allowed to commute – to swap places – when we add or multiply.
concepts.example: A very important warning: the commutative law does not work for subtraction or for division. Look: 10 − 3 = 7, but 3 − 10 = −7. Those are different answers, so subtraction is not commutative. In the same way, 12 ÷ 3 = 4, but 3 ÷ 12 = 0.25. Again, different answers, so division is not commutative. Order matters a great deal for taking away and for sharing. If Hassan has 10 goats and 3 walk away, he has 7 left; he cannot start with 3 goats and give away 10.

concepts.title: The Associative Law
concepts.explanation:
The associative law says that the grouping does not matter when you add or when you multiply. When there are three or more numbers, you may decide which pair to work out first, and the final answer will be the same.

For addition: (8 + 3) + 4 = 8 + (3 + 4). Check the left side: 11 + 4 = 15. Check the right side: 8 + 7 = 15. Both give 15. For multiplication: (5 × 2) × 3 = 5 × (2 × 3). The left side is 10 × 3 = 30; the right side is 5 × 6 = 30. Both give 30. In symbols, (a + b) + c = a + (b + c) and (a × b) × c = a × (b × c). The little brackets simply show which pair you handle first.

The real power of the associative law is that it lets you hunt for friendly pairs – numbers that combine into a round, easy total. Consider 25 × 9 × 4. Working left to right gives 25 × 9 = 225, then 225 × 4 = 900, which is heavy going. But if we regroup as (25 × 4) × 9, we get 100 × 9 = 900 in a single easy step, because 25 × 4 = 100. Notice we also quietly used the commutative law to move the 4 next to the 25; the two laws often work together.

Two more examples show the same idea. For 50 × 16 × 2, regroup as 50 × 2 × 16 = 100 × 16 = 1,600. For 15 × 17 × 6, regroup as 15 × 6 × 17 = 90 × 17 = 1,530. Each time we searched for the pair that makes a round number, then multiplied by the leftover number last.

To use this law well, it helps to memorise the pairs that make friendly numbers. Here are the most useful ones to keep in your head:

Pairs that make 10: 2 × 5, and 1 × 10.

Pairs that make 100: 4 × 25, 2 × 50, and 10 × 10.

Pairs that make 1000: 8 × 125, 4 × 250, and 20 × 50.
concepts.example: When you see a long multiplication, scan it for one of these hidden pairs. If Zahra sees 8 × 17 × 125, her eyes jump straight to the 8 and the 125, because she knows they make 1000. She works out 8 × 125 = 1000, then 1000 × 17 = 17,000. What looked frightening became a single friendly step.

concepts.title: The Distributive Law
concepts.explanation:
The distributive law lets you break one number apart to make a multiplication easier. It connects multiplication with addition and subtraction. In words: to multiply by a sum, you may multiply by each part and then add the results.

The formula is a × (b + c) = (a × b) + (a × c). For example, 6 × (10 + 3) = (6 × 10) + (6 × 3) = 60 + 18 = 78. Notice that 10 + 3 = 13, so we have really worked out 6 × 13 by splitting the 13 into a friendly 10 and an easy 3.

This is a superb mental-maths tool. Suppose Farah must work out 36 × 8. She splits 36 into 30 + 6, then distributes the 8 across both parts: 36 × 8 = (30 × 8) + (6 × 8) = 240 + 48 = 288. Each little multiplication is easy, and adding them is easy too. The frightening 36 × 8 became two friendly steps.

The distributive law also works with subtraction, which is perfect when a number is just below a round number. To work out 48 × 7, notice that 48 is 50 − 2. Then 48 × 7 = (50 × 7) − (2 × 7) = 350 − 14 = 336. Here the formula is a × (b − c) = (a × b) − (a × c). Another example: 19 × 6 = (20 − 1) × 6 = (20 × 6) − (1 × 6) = 120 − 6 = 114.
concepts.example: Often there is more than one way to split a number, and both are correct. For 37 × 6 you could split 37 as 30 + 7, giving (30 × 6) + (7 × 6) = 180 + 42 = 222. Or you could split 37 as 40 − 3, giving (40 × 6) − (3 × 6) = 240 − 18 = 222. Both roads reach 222, so choose whichever feels easier for you. Learning to choose a good split is a skill that grows with practice.

concepts.title: Order of Operations (BIDMAS)
concepts.explanation:
B – Brackets first: work out anything inside ( ) before anything else.

I – Indices next: powers such as squares, if there are any.

D and M – Division and Multiplication, worked from left to right.

A and S – Addition and Subtraction, worked from left to right.

The key idea is that multiplication and division are stronger than addition and subtraction, so we do them first (unless brackets tell us otherwise). Look at 4 + 9 × 5. A common mistake is to work left to right: 4 + 9 = 13, then 13 × 5 = 65. That is wrong. BIDMAS says multiply first: 9 × 5 = 45, then 4 + 45 = 49. The multiplication is done before the addition because it is the stronger operation.

Let us practise the order carefully with four examples. In 6 + 7 × 9, do the multiplication first: 7 × 9 = 63, then 6 + 63 = 69. In 14 − 2 × 7, multiply first: 2 × 7 = 14, then 14 − 14 = 0. In 54 ÷ 9 + 3, do the division first: 54 ÷ 9 = 6, then 6 + 3 = 9. In 16 ÷ 8 + 4, divide first: 16 ÷ 8 = 2, then 2 + 4 = 6. In every case the × or ÷ came before the + or −.

Brackets are the boss of BIDMAS: whatever sits inside them is done first, even if it is only an addition. Compare two calculations that use the same numbers. Without brackets, 4 + 9 × 5 = 49 (multiply first). With brackets, (4 + 9) × 5 = 13 × 5 = 65, because the brackets force us to add before we multiply. This is how brackets let us change the order deliberately when we need a different answer.
concepts.example: When two operations are of equal strength – such as a multiplication and a division together, or an addition and a subtraction together – we simply work from left to right. For example, 20 ÷ 4 × 2 is done as (20 ÷ 4) × 2 = 5 × 2 = 10, moving left to right. A handy rhyme some learners use is 'Brackets, Indices, Divide/Multiply, Add/Subtract'. Whatever you use, the order is always the same.

concepts.title: Choosing the Best Method
concepts.explanation:
Now that you know the laws, the real skill is choosing which one to use. Before you calculate, pause and ask yourself four questions:

Can I use the commutative law to swap to an easier order?

Can I use the associative law to group a friendly pair together?

Can I use the distributive law to break a number apart?

Do I recognise any pattern that makes the work quick?

Take 54 × 6. One method is to split 54 as 50 + 4: 54 × 6 = (50 × 6) + (4 × 6) = 300 + 24 = 324. Another method is to split 54 as 60 − 6: 54 × 6 = (60 × 6) − (6 × 6) = 360 − 36 = 324. Both are correct; you choose the split you find friendlier. For 22 × 3, split 22 as 20 + 2: (20 × 3) + (2 × 3) = 60 + 6 = 66.

Multiplying by 5 has some lovely shortcuts, because 5 is half of 10. To work out 42 × 5 you can multiply by 10 and then halve: 42 × 10 = 420, and 420 ÷ 2 = 210. Or you can halve first and then multiply by 10: 42 ÷ 2 = 21, and 21 × 10 = 210. Or you can distribute: 42 × 5 = (40 + 2) × 5 = 200 + 10 = 210. Three different roads, one answer – pick the one that suits your mind.
concepts.example: A wise habit is to estimate first. Before you work out 42 × 5 exactly, you might think 'about 40 × 5 = 200', so your answer should be near 200. When you land on 210, the closeness tells you to trust it. If you had somehow got 2,100, the huge gap would warn you that something went wrong. Estimating and calculating work together like two hands: one guesses, the other checks.

methods.title: How to use the distributive law
steps: Split the awkward number into a round number plus or minus a small number.
Multiply each part by the other number.
Add (or subtract) the two results.
Check your answer is close to a quick estimate.

methods.title: How to follow BIDMAS
steps: Do anything inside Brackets first.
Work out any Indices (powers).
Do Division and Multiplication, left to right.
Do Addition and Subtraction, left to right.

methods.title: Can I break a number apart with the distributive law?
methods.example: Work out 47 × 8 using the distributive law.
steps: Estimate first, then calculate, then check.
Split one number into two friendly parts (like tens and ones) and multiply each part separately.
Check by adding your two partial answers together and comparing the total to your estimate.

methods.title: Distributive law with subtraction
methods.example: Work out 29 × 6 using the distributive law.
steps: 29 is close to 30, so split it as 30 − 1.
Rounding up to 30 made the first step very easy.

methods.title: Order of operations
steps: BIDMAS says multiply before you add.
First 6 × 4 = 24.
If you had added first you would have got 44, which is wrong.

methods.title: Brackets change the order
methods.example: Work out (7 + 3) × 6 and compare it with 7 + 3 × 6.
steps: With brackets, do inside first: 7 + 3 = 10, then 10 × 6 = 60.
Without brackets, multiply first: 3 × 6 = 18, then 7 + 18 = 25.
The brackets completely change the answer, from 25 to 60.

workedExamples.title: Commutative law to reorder
workedExamples.solution: Counting on 79 from 6 is slow, so swap the order: 6 + 79 = 79 + 6. Now count on 6 from 79: 79 + 6 = 85. The commutative law let us start from the larger number.

workedExamples.title: Associative law to group a friendly pair
workedExamples.solution: Look for a friendly pair. 50 × 2 = 100. Regroup as (50 × 2) × 17 = 100 × 17 = 1,700. Grouping the 50 and 2 first turned a hard sum into an easy one.

workedExamples.title: Distributive law with addition
workedExamples.prompt: Work out 47 × 8 using the distributive law.
workedExamples.solution: Split 47 into 40 + 7. Then 47 × 8 = (40 × 8) + (7 × 8) = 320 + 56 = 376. Remember to multiply *both* parts by 8.

workedExamples.title: Distributive law with subtraction
workedExamples.prompt: Work out 29 × 6 using the distributive law.
workedExamples.solution: 29 is close to 30, so split it as 30 − 1. Then 29 × 6 = (30 × 6) − (1 × 6) = 180 − 6 = 174. Rounding up to 30 made the first step very easy.

workedExamples.title: Order of operations
workedExamples.solution: BIDMAS says multiply before you add. First 6 × 4 = 24. Then 5 + 24 = 29. If you had added first you would have got 44, which is wrong.

workedExamples.title: Brackets change the order
workedExamples.prompt: Work out (7 + 3) × 6 and compare it with 7 + 3 × 6.
workedExamples.solution: With brackets, do inside first: 7 + 3 = 10, then 10 × 6 = 60. Without brackets, multiply first: 3 × 6 = 18, then 7 + 18 = 25. The brackets completely change the answer, from 25 to 60.

workedExamples.title: Choose the best method
workedExamples.solution: Spot the friendly pair 4 × 25 = 100. Reorder and regroup: (4 × 25) × 27 = 100 × 27 = 2,700. Here the commutative and associative laws worked together.

workedExamples.title: Find and fix the error
workedExamples.prompt: Sagal writes: 18 ÷ 6 + 2 = 18 ÷ 8 = 2.25. What went wrong, and what is the correct answer?
workedExamples.solution: Sagal added 6 + 2 first, but BIDMAS says division comes before addition. The division must be done first: 18 ÷ 6 = 3, then 3 + 2 = 5. The correct answer is 5.

workedExamples.title: Work out, doing the brackets first
workedExamples.prompt: Work out, doing the brackets first: a) (8 + 4) × 3 b) 24 ÷ (3 + 1) c) 15 − (6 + 2).

activities.title: Law Detective (Investigation)
steps: Test the commutative law for addition: work out 15 + 27 and 27 + 15. Are they equal?
Test it for multiplication: work out 8 × 12 and 12 × 8. Are they equal?
Now test subtraction: work out 20 − 8 and 8 − 20. Are they equal?
Write a short 'detective report': which operations follow the commutative law, and which do not? Give an example for each.
You have just proved, with your own numbers, why the law works for + and × but not for − and ÷.

activities.title: Friendly-Pair Card Game
activities.materials: small cards with the numbers 2, 4, 5, 8, 10, 25, 50, 125 written on them.
steps: Shuffle the cards and place them face down.
Turn over two cards and multiply them together.
If the two make a round number (10, 100 or 1000), you win a point and keep the pair.
Play until the cards run out. The player with the most friendly pairs wins.
This game trains your eyes to spot the pairs that make the associative law so powerful.

activities.title: BIDMAS Treasure Hunt
activities.materials: paper, a pencil, and coloured pencils for highlighting.
steps: Write out these expressions: 5 + 3 × 4; 12 − 2 × 3; (8 + 4) × 3; 24 ÷ (3 + 1) + 7.
For each one, highlight the operation you must do first in one colour.
Solve each expression step by step, writing every stage.
Check with your AI tutor or a family member. Did the brackets change any answers?

activities.title: Distributive Law Rectangles
activities.materials: squared or dotted paper and coloured pencils.
steps: Draw a rectangle 6 squares tall and 13 squares wide. This shows 6 × 13.
Draw a line to split the width into 10 and 3, making two smaller rectangles.
Colour one part and count its squares (6 × 10 = 60); colour the other (6 × 3 = 18).
Add the two parts: 60 + 18 = 78. Check it equals 6 × 13. You have drawn the distributive law!

activities.title: Market Maths (Family Task)
activities.materials: a family member (or your AI tutor) and some real or pretend prices in shillings.
steps: Ask a family member to name a shopping list, for example 4 items at 25 shillings each.
Use a friendly pair or the distributive law to work out the total in your head.
Say your method out loud: 'I grouped the 4 and the 25 to make 100.'
Swap roles and let your family member try a calculation while you check it.

activities.title: Number Trick Show
activities.materials: paper, a pencil, and a friend or your AI tutor to amaze.
steps: Ask your friend to pick any two-digit number in secret.
Tell them: multiply it by 5, add 36, multiply by 20, then tell you the result.
You subtract 720 in your head, and announce their number multiplied by 100.
Explain the trick using the laws: multiplying by 5 then 20 is the same as multiplying by 100.
Understanding *why* the trick works is more impressive than the trick itself – that is real mathematical power.

rules.title: The Commutative Law
rules.text: Commutative Law Order does not matter for adding or multiplying. a + b = b + a and a x b = b x a. It does NOT work for subtraction or division.

rules.title: The Associative Law
rules.text: Associative Law Grouping does not matter for adding or multiplying. (a + b) + c = a + (b + c) and (a x b) x c = a x (b x c). Use it to group friendly pairs like 4 x 25 = 100.

rules.title: The Distributive Law
rules.text: Distributive Law Break a number apart to multiply it more easily. a x (b + c) = (a x b) + (a x c). a x (b - c) = (a x b) - (a x c).

rules.title: BIDMAS: The Order of Operations
rules.text: Order of Operations (BIDMAS) Brackets, Indices, Division and Multiplication, Addition and Subtraction. Do x and division before + and subtraction. When operations are equally strong, work left to right.

rules.title: Friendly Pairs to Memorise
rules.text: 4 × 25 = 100, 2 × 50 = 100, 10 × 10 = 100, 8 × 125 = 1,000, 4 × 250 = 1,000, 20 × 5 = 100. Spotting these pairs makes the associative law easy to use.

realProblems.prompt: Hassan buys 6 goats at the market. Each goat costs 48 shillings... hundred, that is 4800 shillings each. Use the distributive law to work out 48 × 6 first (the price in hundreds).
realProblems.answer: 48 × 6 = (50 − 2) × 6 = 300 − 12 = 288 (hundreds of shillings), so 28,800 shillings in total for 6 goats.
realProblems.hint: Decide which idea the question is really about (Commutative law, Associative law, Distributive law), then work one step at a time and check the answer is sensible.

realProblems.prompt: A classroom at Nuur Academy has 6 rows of desks. Each row has 4 desks, and there are 5 extra desks at the back. Work out 6 × 4 + 5 using BIDMAS to find the total number of desks.
realProblems.answer: 6 × 4 = 24 (multiply first under BIDMAS), then 24 + 5 = 29 desks in total.

realProblems.prompt: Omar works out 100 − 6 × 8 to find how many mangoes are left after selling. What is the correct answer, and why is it not 752?
realProblems.answer: 52 mangoes are left. Multiply first: 6 × 8 = 48, then 100 − 48 = 52. The wrong answer 752 comes from subtracting first (100 − 6 = 94) and then multiplying by 8, which breaks BIDMAS.

reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Marcus subtracted 1 instead of 1 × 4 = 4; correct is 80 − 4 = 76.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Show, using the distributive law, that 12 × (5 + 3) = (12 × 5) + (12 × 3). Work out both sides.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Left side: 12 × 8 = 96. Right side: 60 + 36 = 96. Both equal 96.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Amina says 'You can always swap the numbers around in any calculation.' Is she right? Give an example that proves your point.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: No – swapping only works for + and ×; for example 10 − 3 = 7 but 3 − 10 = −7.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Put brackets into 4 + 6 × 2 to make the answer 20 instead of 16.
Explain the key idea in Choosing the Best Method.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Now that you know the laws, the real skill is choosing which one to use. Before you calculate, pause and ask yourself four questions: Can I use the commutative law to swap to an easier order?

questions.question: Work out 6 + 79 the easy way.
questions.hint: Work it out step by step, using the Unit 17 methods.
questions.explanation: Counting on 79 from 6 is slow, so swap the order: 6 + 79 = 79 + 6. Now count on 6 from 79: 79 + 6 = 85. The commutative law let us start from the larger number.

questions.question: Work out 50 × 17 × 2.
questions.hint: Work it out step by step, using the Unit 17 methods.
questions.explanation: Look for a friendly pair. 50 × 2 = 100. Regroup as (50 × 2) × 17 = 100 × 17 = 1,700. Grouping the 50 and 2 first turned a hard sum into an easy one.

questions.question: Work out 47 × 8 using the distributive law.
questions.hint: Work it out step by step, using the Unit 17 methods.
questions.explanation: Split 47 into 40 + 7. Then 47 × 8 = (40 × 8) + (7 × 8) = 320 + 56 = 376. Remember to multiply *both* parts by 8.

questions.question: Work out 29 × 6 using the distributive law.
questions.hint: Work it out step by step, using the Unit 17 methods.
questions.explanation: 29 is close to 30, so split it as 30 − 1. Then 29 × 6 = (30 × 6) − (1 × 6) = 180 − 6 = 174. Rounding up to 30 made the first step very easy.

questions.question: Work out 4 × 27 × 25 efficiently.
questions.hint: Work it out step by step, using the Unit 17 methods.
questions.explanation: Spot the friendly pair 4 × 25 = 100. Reorder and regroup: (4 × 25) × 27 = 100 × 27 = 2,700. Here the commutative and associative laws worked together.

selfAssessment: I can use the commutative law to reorder additions and multiplications and make them easier.
I can use the associative law to regroup numbers so that friendly pairs come together.
I can use the distributive law to break a number apart for quick mental multiplication.
I can follow the correct order of operations using BIDMAS.
I can explain why each law works, and know when it does and does not apply.
I can spot and correct common calculation errors using mathematical reasoning.
I can choose the most efficient method for any calculation you meet.
